title: The Brothers Karamazov, Part 2
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
summary: Na primeira parte, os irmãos Karamazov voltaram para casa e o ódio entre Dmitri e o pai, rivais pelo amor de Grushenka, chegou ao limite. Agora Ivan decide partir para Moscou depois de uma conversa enigmática com o criado Smerdyakov, enquanto Alyosha vê seu amado mestre Zosima morrer e atravessa uma crise de fé. Desesperado para conseguir três mil rublos, Dmitri corre pela cidade numa noite febril que mudará para sempre o destino da família.

chapters.title: A Talk at the Gate
paragraphs: On his way home that night, Ivan felt an anxiety he could not explain. It was not because of his talk with Alyosha, nor because he was leaving tomorrow. It was something else, something disgusting, like a small irritating object lying somewhere in his mind. When he reached his father's gate, he suddenly understood what it was. On the bench by the gate sat Smerdyakov, enjoying the evening air, and the moment Ivan saw him, he knew that this was the man who had been troubling his soul.
Ivan wanted to pass by without a word. But Smerdyakov stood up, and something in his face, a kind of sly, knowing look, made Ivan stop. He hated himself for stopping.

Smerdyakov was dressed with his usual care, in a clean shirt and polished boots, and his thin yellow face looked older than his twenty-four years. Ivan had often talked with him during the summer. At first he had found the young man interesting: he asked strange questions about how there could be light on the first day of creation, when the sun, moon and stars were only made on the fourth. But Ivan soon saw that it was not God that Smerdyakov cared about. He had an endless, hidden vanity, and he seemed to think that he and Ivan shared some kind of secret understanding. Lately this familiarity had begun to disgust Ivan.
“Is the master still asleep?” Ivan asked, quietly and against his own will.
“Still asleep, sir.” Smerdyakov paused, and then said, with a little smile, “I wonder at you, sir.”
“Why do you wonder at me?”
“Why don't you go to Chermashnya, sir?” Chermashnya was a village where Fyodor Pavlovich owned some woodland, and the old man had been begging Ivan to go there and sell it for him.
“Why should I go to Chermashnya?”
“Your father has been asking you so much, sir.”
Ivan sat down on the bench beside him, though his whole body was shaking with irritation. “Speak plainly. What do you want?”

Smerdyakov lowered his voice. “I'm in a terrible position, Ivan Fyodorovich. I don't know how to help myself. Your brother Dmitri Fyodorovich keeps coming to me and asking: has she come? Is she coming? And he says that if I don't tell him at once when she comes, he'll kill me first. And your father, every night, locks himself in and makes me promise to watch for her. We've agreed on signals. Two quick knocks and then a third, slower, means that Agrafena Alexandrovna has come. And another, three quick knocks, means something urgent. Nobody knows these signals except your father and me. And now your brother knows them, because I told him.”
“Why did you tell him?”
“Out of fear, sir. How could I not tell him? And now I feel that tomorrow I'm going to have a long fit.”
“What do you mean, a long fit? Can you tell in advance?”

“One can't tell in advance, of course. But tomorrow I'll be going down to the cellar for something, and I might fall down the steps. That's how fits often come. Something tells me I'll have a long one, a day or two, maybe three.”
Ivan stared at him. “You're pretending! You want to pretend to have a fit so that you can't be blamed.”

“If I could pretend, sir, which is easy for a man with experience, I'd have every right to save myself from death that way. Because if I'm lying ill, then even if Agrafena Alexandrovna comes to your father, your brother can't blame me for not telling him.”
“And Grigory? Grigory will be on guard.”

“Grigory Vasilyevich has a pain in his back. Marfa Ignatievna makes him a medicine of strong vodka and a secret herb. She rubs his back with it, and then he drinks the rest and falls into such a sleep that he hears nothing till morning. And she drinks a little too, and sleeps like the dead. Tomorrow, sir, she intends to give him the treatment.”
Ivan felt a cold weight in his chest. “And if Dmitri comes, and he hears the signal, and the door is opened...”

“That's just it, sir. Your father has three thousand roubles in that envelope with the pink ribbon. And your brother says the money is his. And your father has drawn up no will. If he dies, sir, each of his three sons gets forty thousand roubles, perhaps more. But if he marries Agrafena Alexandrovna, she'll have everything, and nothing will be left for you. That's why it would be better for you, sir, to go to Chermashnya, or even to Moscow. It wouldn't be good for you to be here.”
Ivan stood up suddenly, as if he were going to strike him. Smerdyakov stepped back. Then, without a word, Ivan laughed strangely, turned, and went through the gate.

chapters.title: A Clever Man's Advice
paragraphs: That night Ivan could not sleep. He went out several times onto the dark stairway and listened to his father moving about downstairs, muttering, walking from room to room. He did not know why he listened. Later he called it the most despicable moment of his life.

He remembered afterwards how, at about two in the morning, he had stood on the stairs for five minutes, holding his breath, his heart beating, trying to hear what the old man was doing. He was not curious. He was not afraid. It was something else, a strange, shameful eagerness that he could not name and did not want to name. Then he went back to bed and slept heavily, as if he had been beaten.

In the morning he told his father that he was leaving for Moscow. The old man was upset, then cunning. “Do me a favour, Ivan. Go by way of Chermashnya. It's only a little out of your way. There's a merchant there, Gorstkin, who wants to buy my woods. Just look at him and tell me if he's lying. If he strokes his beard while he talks, he's telling the truth. If he holds it with his left hand and grins, he's cheating. You'll write to me.”
“Very well,” said Ivan, with a cold smile. “I'll go to your Chermashnya.”

The old man was delighted. He kissed his son, gave him a little brandy for the road, and stood on the steps waving. “Come back soon, Ivan! Remember, you're always welcome. I'll be glad to see you, I really will.” There was something almost touching in the way he said it, as if he were afraid of being left alone. Ivan did not turn round.
Ivan, to his own surprise, agreed. Then, as the carriage was about to leave, Smerdyakov came out to see him off.
“You see, I'm going to Chermashnya,” Ivan said, without knowing why he said it.
“So it's true what they say,” said Smerdyakov, looking at him meaningfully. “It's always worth talking to a clever man.”
Ivan drove away. At the first station, however, he changed his mind and did not go to Chermashnya. He went straight on to the railway and to Moscow.

All the way to the railway he felt a strange lightness, as if he had escaped from something. He looked at the fields, the birds and the wide sky, and he told himself that he was leaving it all behind for ever, his father, Dmitri, Katerina Ivanovna, Smerdyakov and the whole stinking nest. But under the lightness there was something else, a dark, cold feeling that he did not want to look at. He kept seeing Smerdyakov's face at the gate, and that knowing little smile. At seven o'clock that evening, as the train started, he whispered to himself, “I am a scoundrel.”

That same afternoon, as he had predicted, Smerdyakov went down to the cellar for something, fell down the steps, and had a terrible epileptic fit. They found him at the bottom, twisting and foaming at the mouth. A doctor was called and declared that it was a serious attack and might last a long time. Marfa put him to bed in the little room next to her own. And that same evening Grigory, whose back had been hurting him all day, asked his wife for his famous treatment.

chapters.title: The Elder's Last Words
paragraphs: While all this was happening at his father's house, Alyosha was at the monastery, by Father Zosima's bed. The old man was very weak, but that evening he felt a little better and was able to sit up in his chair and speak with his closest friends among the monks for the last time. He spoke more than he had for a long time, as if he wanted to give them everything that remained in his heart. Alyosha later wrote down much of what he said.

Before he began, the elder turned to Alyosha. “Did you see your brother Dmitri? Did you find him?” Alyosha said that he had not, that he had looked for him everywhere. “Hurry, then,” said the old man. “Go tomorrow, and look again. Perhaps you will still be able to prevent something terrible. I bowed yesterday to his great future suffering.” Then he added, more softly, “You remind me of my brother Markel. That is why I loved you from the first moment. Let me tell you about him.”

He talked first of his elder brother, Markel, who had died at seventeen of consumption. “He was a proud boy who laughed at religion. But when he became ill, everything changed in him. He would say to our mother: Mother, my joy, don't cry. Life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we won't see it. If we would only see it, tomorrow there would be heaven all over the world. And he said: Each of us is guilty before everyone, for everyone and for everything, and I more than all. Our mother smiled through her tears and said: How can you be more guilty than all? There are murderers and robbers. And he said: Mother, little heart of mine, believe me, each of us is truly guilty before all and for all. I don't know how to explain it, but I feel it so strongly that it hurts. He even asked the little birds to forgive him.”

The elder smiled. “I was a child then. Later I forgot it. I became an officer, a wild, cruel young man. I drank, I fought, I was proud of my uniform. I fell in love with a beautiful young lady, and when she married someone else, I decided to challenge her husband to a duel. The night before the duel I came home in a terrible mood and struck my servant, Afanasy, twice in the face with all my strength, until his face was covered with blood. He stood there at attention, with his arms at his sides, and he didn't even raise a hand to protect himself.

“In the morning I woke early. The sun was shining, the birds were singing. And suddenly I felt a shame in my heart, as if something vile were there. I remembered Afanasy standing there and taking my blows like a soldier. What had I done? And then I remembered Markel's words: each of us is guilty before all. I ran to Afanasy's room and fell at his feet. Forgive me, I said. He was horrified. Then I went to the duel. I let my opponent fire first. He shot, and the bullet only grazed my cheek. Then I threw my pistol into the trees. Gentlemen, I said, forgive me. Look around you at God's gifts, the clear sky, the pure air. Only we are sinful and foolish, and we don't understand that life is paradise. My fellow officers were furious. They thought I was a coward and a disgrace to the regiment. But I resigned, and soon afterwards I became a monk.”

Then he spoke of a mysterious visitor who had come to him in those days, a respected and wealthy man of the town. This man came night after night, until one evening he confessed a terrible secret: fourteen years earlier, he had murdered a young widow he loved, and another man, a servant, had been blamed and had died before the trial. Since then he had married and had children, and was admired by everyone, but he could not live with his secret. Zosima told him to confess publicly. At last the man stood up at his own birthday party and declared his crime. Nobody believed him. They decided he had gone mad.

“I have done my duty,” he whispered to Zosima when the young monk visited him on his deathbed. “I feel joy and peace for the first time in fourteen years. God has had mercy on me.” Zosima said that he learned more from that man than from many books: he learned how heavy a hidden sin can be, and how much courage it takes to lay it down. A few days later he fell ill and died, at peace.

“Brothers,” said the elder, “do not be afraid of men's sins. Love a man even in his sin, for that is the likeness of divine love. Love all of God's creation, every grain of sand. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will understand the divine mystery in things. And do not judge anyone. A man cannot judge, for he himself may be guilty of the very crime of the one who stands before him. Fathers and teachers, I ask myself: what is hell? And I answer: it is the suffering of being unable to love.”

Late that night, he suddenly felt a sharp pain in his chest. He slipped from his chair onto the floor, stretched out his arms as if to embrace the earth, and, kneeling with his face to the ground, quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

chapters.title: The Odour of Corruption
paragraphs: The news of the elder's death spread through the monastery and the town before dawn. Crowds of people came, believing that miracles would happen at the body of such a holy man. Mothers brought sick children. Everyone expected some sign. Alyosha, worn out with grief, spent the night near the coffin, where a monk was reading the Gospel aloud.

The monks prepared the body according to the ancient rules. They did not wash it with water, but wiped it with a sponge. They dressed the elder in his monk's robes, put a cross in his hands and covered his face with a black cloth. In the morning they placed him in a coffin in the large front room of his cell. Through the open windows came the noise of the crowd, growing louder every hour. Some had brought bottles of sand and oil, hoping to collect something holy. Everyone was waiting.

But by the afternoon of the next day something happened that no one had expected. From the coffin, at first faintly and then more and more clearly, there came a smell of corruption. The elder's body was decaying, and decaying sooner than nature itself might have required. It was as though nature had decided to humiliate him.

To ordinary people this would have meant nothing. But in the monastery the bodies of truly holy men were not supposed to decay. Many monks had envied Zosima, many had disliked his gentle, new ways. Now they began to whisper, and then to speak openly.

“His teaching was false,” said one. “He taught that life is a great joy and not humble suffering. He ate cherry jam with his tea. He allowed people to go to him for confession and treated it like a sacrament.”
“God has given a sign,” said another, with satisfaction.

An old fanatic monk, Father Ferapont, who lived in a hut in the woods, eating nothing but bread and talking to devils, burst into the cell. He waved his arms over the coffin and shouted, “Out, Satan, out!” Then he cried that the dead man had not kept the fasts, and that that was why he stank. He was led out, but the scandal grew all day long.

Alyosha felt something break inside him. It was not that he had expected a miracle for himself. He wanted justice. He could not bear that the man he loved more than anyone in the world, who had been raised above all others, should now be shamed and mocked, and that this should come from Providence itself. Where was the finger of God? Why had God hidden His face at the moment when it was needed most?

Father Paissy, the gentle and learned monk who had been Zosima's closest friend, saw Alyosha leaving the cell and stopped him. “Where are you going, my son? Are you leaving the coffin? Are you one of those of little faith too?” Alyosha looked at him strangely, waved his hand without a word, and walked quickly out of the gate. Father Paissy watched him go, and he sighed. He understood that something important was happening in the young man's soul, and he prayed for him.
In the evening Rakitin found him lying face down on the grass in the woods near the monastery.
“So you're here, Alyosha! What's the matter? Have you rebelled against your God? Is it because your old man began to stink? Did you really believe he'd do miracles?”
“I'm not rebelling against my God,” said Alyosha with a strange smile. “I simply don't accept His world.” It was Ivan's phrase, and Rakitin, who did not know that, looked at him in surprise.
“Well, well! Our quiet one has changed. Will you eat some sausage, then? And drink vodka?”
“Give me vodka too.”
“Is that true? Then come with me. I'll take you somewhere better than vodka. To Grushenka. She's asked me many times to bring you to her. Will you go?”

“Let's go,” said Alyosha. Rakitin could hardly believe his luck. Grushenka had promised him twenty-five roubles if he brought her the young monk, and Rakitin was delighted, too, at the thought of seeing the saint fall.

chapters.title: The Onion
paragraphs: Grushenka was waiting in her room, dressed in black silk, lying on her sofa as if she expected someone. She jumped up in fright when they came in, and then laughed with joy when she saw who it was.

“Alyosha! Is it really you? Rakitin, you brought him! Oh, I thought it was someone else. I'm waiting for news, you see. I'm waiting for a message. Sit down, Alyosha, sit down. I'm so glad. What shall I give you? Champagne? Rakitin, go and fetch the champagne, I'll pay for it. Today's a special day.”
She was excited and restless, and before Alyosha knew what was happening, she had sat down on his knees, like a playful kitten, and put her arm round his neck.
“You don't mind, do you? I'll make you merry. You're so sad, my little monk.”

Alyosha did not push her away. Strangely, he felt none of the fear or temptation he would once have felt. The great grief in his heart had swallowed everything else. He looked at her with curiosity, and even with something like tenderness.
“Don't tease him,” said Rakitin. “His elder died this morning, Father Zosima.”

Grushenka jumped off his knees at once and crossed herself. “Father Zosima is dead? Oh, God, and I didn't know! And I was sitting on his knees! Forgive me, Alyosha.” She moved away and sat on the sofa, suddenly serious.

“Rakitin,” said Alyosha quietly, “don't sneer at her. You see how she pitied me. I came here expecting to find a wicked soul, and I found a true sister, a treasure, a loving soul. She pitied me just now. Agrafena Alexandrovna, I'm speaking of you. You've restored my soul.”

Grushenka's lips trembled. “He's saved me too,” she said. “I'm a wicked woman, Alyosha. I wanted to ruin you. I wanted to swallow you up and laugh. I even promised Rakitin money if he brought you. But you came, and you called me sister. Listen. Let me tell you a little story, a fable. I heard it from our cook when I was a child.

“Once upon a time there was a very wicked old woman, and she died. She hadn't done a single good deed in her whole life. So the devils took her and threw her into the lake of fire. Her guardian angel stood there and wondered what good deed he could remember, to tell God. Then he remembered and said: she once pulled up an onion in her garden and gave it to a beggar woman. And God said to him: take that onion, then, and hold it out to her in the lake, and let her take hold of it, and if you can pull her out, let her come to Paradise. But if the onion breaks, she must stay where she is.

“So the angel ran to the woman and held out the onion. Here, he said, catch hold, and I'll pull you out. And he began carefully pulling her out. He had just pulled her nearly out when the other sinners in the lake saw what was happening and began clinging to her, to be pulled out with her. And she was a very wicked woman, and she began kicking them. I'm to be pulled out, not you. It's my onion, not yours! As soon as she said that, the onion broke. And the woman fell back into the lake, and she's burning there to this day. And the angel wept and went away.
“That's me, Alyosha. I've only given one little onion in all my life. That's all the good I've ever done.”

She laughed through her tears. “And do you know what my onion was today? I wanted to ruin you, but when I heard that your elder had died, I got off your knees. That's all. That was my little onion. Don't praise me, Alyosha, don't think I'm good. I'm wicked, very wicked. If you praise me, I'll be ashamed.”
“I gave you an onion too,” said Alyosha, smiling. “A very little one. That's all.” Rakitin, sitting in the corner with his champagne, snorted with contempt, but neither of them looked at him.

Then she told them her secret. Five years ago, at seventeen, she had been seduced by a Polish officer, who had abandoned her. She had wept all night for years, and she had sworn to have her revenge on him. Now he was a widower, and he had written to her. He was waiting for her at Mokroye.
“I've been waiting all day for his message. And I don't know yet what I'll do. I may go to him like a little dog, or I may take a knife with me. I don't know!”

At that moment a carriage drove into the yard, and a servant ran in with a note. Grushenka read it and went pale. “He's sent for me! He's whistling for me, and I'll crawl to him like a little dog.” She ran to get her cloak. Then she turned in the doorway.

“Alyosha, give my greetings to your brother Mitya. Tell him not to remember evil against me. And tell him that Grushenka loved him for one little hour, only one hour, and that he must remember that hour all his life. Tell him Grushenka said so!”
And she was gone, the bells of the carriage ringing in the dark.

Rakitin was furious. He had not got his money, and the scene had not gone as he had planned. “So, you converted a sinner. Turned a harlot to the path of truth, cast out seven devils. You've done a miracle after all!” he said, and walked off in another direction, leaving Alyosha alone.

chapters.title: Cana of Galilee
paragraphs: It was late when Alyosha returned to the monastery. He went to the cell where the elder's coffin stood. The windows were open, and the air was fresher, though the smell had not gone. Father Paissy was reading the Gospel over the coffin, and only a few monks remained. Alyosha knelt down in a corner and began to pray, but his thoughts drifted. He felt a sweet, quiet peace in his heart for the first time since the morning.

The bitterness of the day had gone, though the grief remained. He no longer felt that God had betrayed his elder. He remembered the old man's face, his gentle smile, his words about joy, and he understood that the smell of the body could not touch any of that. Whatever the monks were whispering, what Zosima had given him could not decay. He thought of Grushenka and her onion, and of how she had pitied him. Then he listened to the reading.

It was the story of the wedding at Cana of Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine. Alyosha half dozed as he listened. “They have no wine,” said the mother of Jesus. And Alyosha thought sleepily: Ah, how lovely. He did not come to people's grief, but to their joy. He helped them in their joy. Whoever loves men loves their joy too. The elder used to say that.

Then the room seemed to widen. Alyosha saw a wedding feast, guests, the young couple, tables covered with food, and the wine-steward tasting the new wine. And among the guests he saw a little old man rise and come towards him. It was Father Zosima, in his ordinary clothes, smiling, with his face shining.

“Yes, my dear, I've been called to the feast too,” said the elder. “Why are you hiding here? Come and join us. We are rejoicing, drinking new wine, the wine of a new and great joy. Do you see how many guests there are? Here is the bridegroom and the bride, and here is the wise steward tasting the wine. Why are you looking at me so surprised? I gave an onion to a beggar, so I'm here too. And many here have given only an onion each, only one little onion. What are all our deeds? And you, my gentle one, you too have given an onion today to a woman who was hungry. Begin your work, my dear, begin it, gentle one!”
Something burned in Alyosha's heart and filled it till it ached. Tears of rapture rose from his soul. He stretched out his hands, cried out, and woke up.
The coffin was there again, Father Paissy was reading, the open window was full of darkness. Alyosha stood for a moment, then turned and walked out of the cell, down the steps and into the night.

The vault of heaven, full of soft shining stars, stretched wide and endless above him. The Milky Way ran in two pale streams from the zenith to the horizon. The fresh, motionless, still night covered the earth. The white towers and golden domes of the cathedral gleamed against the sapphire sky. The autumn flowers in the beds near the house were sleeping till morning. The silence of the earth seemed to melt into the silence of the heavens.

Alyosha stood, gazed, and suddenly threw himself down flat on the earth. He did not know why he embraced it. He could not have told why he longed so to kiss it, to kiss it all. But he kissed it weeping, sobbing and watering it with his tears, and he vowed passionately to love it, to love it for ever and ever. “Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears,” echoed in his soul. He wanted to forgive everyone and for everything, and to beg forgiveness, not for himself, but for all men, for all and for everything.

He had fallen on the earth a weak boy, but he rose up a resolute fighter, and he knew and felt it at once, in that minute of rapture. Never, never, all his life long, could Alyosha forget that minute. “Someone visited my soul in that hour,” he used to say afterwards, with firm faith in his words.
Three days later he left the monastery, as his elder had told him to do, to go out into the world.

chapters.title: Three Thousand Roubles
paragraphs: During those same two days, Dmitri had been rushing about the town and the district like a man possessed. He had one fixed idea: he must find three thousand roubles at once. With that money he would repay Katerina Ivanovna, wipe out his disgrace, and take Grushenka away to start a new life far from here, somewhere in Siberia or anywhere at all, if only she would choose him. Without it, he was a thief, and he could not go to Grushenka as a thief.

His first idea was Kuzma Samsonov, the rich old merchant who had been Grushenka's protector for years. Samsonov was now dying, with swollen legs, but he still ruled his household like a tyrant. Dmitri went to him early in the morning, dressed in his best coat, and stood before the old man in his huge, gloomy drawing room.

“I have come to you with a business proposal,” Dmitri began nervously, and he explained at length that he had a claim to his father's property, perhaps worth twenty-eight thousand roubles, and that he was ready to give up all his rights to Samsonov for only three thousand. Samsonov could then take the old man to court and win a fortune.
Samsonov listened with a cold, unmoving face. When Dmitri finished, he was silent for a long time. Then he said, “Excuse me, we don't undertake such business.”
Dmitri felt his legs grow weak. “Then I am lost. Kuzma Kuzmich, is there no way?”

The old man thought, and a strange gleam came into his eyes. “There's a man,” he said slowly. “A peasant called Lyagavy, a dealer in timber. He's been haggling with your father over the woods at Chermashnya for a year. Your father won't agree on the price. If you went to him and offered him what you've offered me, he might accept. He's staying in the village of Sukhoy Possyolok just now.”

Dmitri was overwhelmed with gratitude. He did not realise that the old man, who hated him, had simply decided to make fun of him. He pawned his watch for six roubles, borrowed three more from his landlady, hired a cart and drove off towards the village. He had not eaten all day.

He arrived after dark at a hut deep in the forest, where the priest of the village had taken him. There, on a bench, lay a big peasant with a red face, snoring. It was Lyagavy, and he was completely drunk. Dmitri shook him, shouted at him, tried to pour water on his face, all in vain. He decided to wait until morning.

The hut was stuffy and hot, and the stove had been lit badly. Dmitri sat on a bench and fell asleep, and woke with a splitting headache. The room was full of charcoal fumes. He had nearly been poisoned. He opened the windows and spent half the night bringing himself and the peasant back to their senses, wetting the drunkard's head with cold water.
In the morning Lyagavy woke up and began drinking again at once. When Dmitri explained his business, the peasant looked at him with stupid insolence.
“You're lying. You're a dyer.”
“A dyer? I'm Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov! I have a proposal about the woods.”

“You rented the woods and cheated me. You're a scoundrel,” said the peasant, and began to laugh. He was so drunk that he could understand nothing. At last Dmitri understood that Samsonov had sent him there as a joke. He left the hut without his cap, almost weeping with rage and humiliation, and walked for miles through the forest, back towards the road.
“I'm like a man who has been killed,” he thought. “And she, where is she? What if, while I've been here, she's gone to the old man?”

chapters.title: The Pestle
paragraphs: Back in town, the first thing Dmitri did was run to Grushenka's house. She was at home, to his great relief, and she asked him, very sweetly, to walk with her to Samsonov's, where she said she had to go to help him count his money. She asked him to come back for her at midnight. He left her there, happy and reassured.

Then he went to look for money once more. He thought of Madame Khokhlakova, the rich widow who always talked about helping people. She did not like him, but she disliked Katerina Ivanovna's engagement to him even more. Surely she would want to help him get away.

Madame Khokhlakova received him with great excitement. “I knew you would come! I've been expecting you. You've come for three thousand roubles, haven't you? But I'll give you more than three thousand. Infinitely more!”
Dmitri's heart leapt. “You'll save my life! I'll repay you, I swear.”

“I will give you more than three thousand, Dmitri Fyodorovich. I'll give you the gold mines! Why don't you go to the gold mines? I've been watching you walk, and I'm convinced you have the walk of a man who will find gold. You are a practical man, a realist. Go to the mines, and you'll find millions.”
“But madam, the three thousand...”

“Wait, wait!” She ran out of the room and came back with a small silver icon on a chain. She hung it round his neck. “It's from Kiev, it will protect you. There. Now, go to the mines. It's all decided.”
“But the money, madam! You promised!”
“Money? I haven't got any money, Dmitri Fyodorovich. I'm having a quarrel with my estate manager. I've just borrowed five hundred roubles myself. But that doesn't matter. The mines!”

Dmitri struck the table with his fist, spat on the floor, and ran out of the house. In the dark street he wept like a little child. He had nothing left. In his despair he ran back to Samsonov's house to fetch Grushenka early. But the servant there told him that she had left long ago, almost as soon as she had come.
He ran to her house. The old servant woman and the maid, Fenya, were in the kitchen, and they were frightened when they saw his face.
“Where is she?”
“I don't know, Dmitri Fyodorovich, I don't know anything, as God is my witness. She went out...”

He did not wait to hear more. In a flash he understood: she had gone to his father. Everything was clear. The old man had the money, the envelope, the pink ribbon, and she had gone there. On the kitchen table lay a small brass pestle, used for grinding pepper. Without thinking, Dmitri seized it, put it in his pocket, and ran out.
“Oh, Lord, he's going to kill someone!” cried Fenya.

He ran through the dark streets, not along the main road but by the back lanes, towards his father's garden. He knew the way. He climbed over the fence at the same place where poor Lizaveta had once climbed it, and dropped down into the garden. Everything was still. He crept through the bushes towards the house. A light was burning in his father's bedroom window.

chapters.title: In the Dark
paragraphs: Dmitri stood behind a bush in the dark garden and watched the lighted window. The night was warm, with no wind. His heart was beating so hard that he could hardly breathe. He went closer, stepping carefully, and stood at one side of the window, looking in.

His father's bedroom was small and clearly visible. A red screen stood in one corner. Fyodor Pavlovich stood in the middle of the room, in his new striped silk dressing gown, with a clean shirt, as if he were dressed for a celebration. He was alone. He walked restlessly about, then stopped and listened. Twice he went to the window and peered out into the darkness. Then he went to the table, poured himself half a glass of brandy, and drank it.

“He's alone,” thought Dmitri. “She's not here.” But perhaps she was behind the screen? He had to know. He remembered the signals Smerdyakov had told him. He tapped twice on the window frame, quickly, and then a third time, more slowly. It meant: Grushenka has come.
The old man jumped. He ran to the window and threw it open. He thrust out his head and peered into the dark.

“Grushenka, is it you? Is it you?” he said in a trembling whisper. “Where are you, my angel? Where are you?” He was terribly excited, gasping. He leaned further and further out, looking to the right, towards the door, and his neck and his profile were lit up by the lamp behind him. The little bag of skin under his chin, the hooked nose, the lips smiling in greedy expectation, all of it was right there.

At that moment a terrible hatred surged up in Dmitri's heart. “There he was, his rival, his tormentor, the tormentor of his life!” It was that sudden, furious, avenging hatred he had spoken of to Alyosha, as if he had foreseen it four days earlier. He pulled the brass pestle out of his pocket...

“God was watching over me then,” Dmitri said later. For at that very moment, as it happened, Grigory woke up in his little cottage. His back ached, and the medicine had not worked as well as usual. He got up, dressed, and went out into the yard, and, remembering that the garden gate had not been locked, he walked towards it. He was just in time to see a figure running through the dark garden towards the fence.
“Parricide!” he cried, and ran after the figure. He reached the fence just as Dmitri was climbing over it, and caught hold of his leg with both hands.

Dmitri did not think. He struck with the pestle in his hand. The old servant fell down without a sound, his head bleeding. Dmitri jumped back down into the garden and bent over him. He threw the pestle away into the grass. Then he took out his handkerchief and tried to wipe the blood from the old man's head, to see how bad the wound was. The handkerchief was soaked with blood at once, and his own hands were covered with it.

“Is he dead? Have I killed him? If I've killed him, I've killed him,” he said aloud. “The old man's caught it. There you are, then.” Then he climbed back over the fence and ran off into the darkness, towards the town, with the blood-soaked handkerchief crumpled in his fist.

chapters.title: Bloody Hands
paragraphs: Dmitri ran straight back to Grushenka's house. Fenya and the old woman were still in the kitchen. When he burst in, Fenya fell on her knees in terror.
“Where is she?” he shouted, seizing her by the throat. “Where is she now?”
“Dmitri Fyodorovich, dear, don't kill me! I'll tell you everything! She's gone to Mokroye, to her officer!”
“What officer?”

“Her old one, the one who left her five years ago. He's come back, and he sent for her, and she went to him. Alexei Fyodorovich was here with her when the message came. She told me to tell you that she loved you for one little hour, and that you must remember that hour all your life.”
Dmitri let go of her and sat down on a chest. He was silent. All his rage was suddenly gone. His face was white and calm. Fenya, still trembling, looked at his hands.
“Dmitri Fyodorovich, sir, there's blood on your hands! Blood!”

He looked down at his hands as if they belonged to someone else. “Yes, blood,” he said quietly. “That's human blood, Fenya. And my God, why was it shed?” Then he got up and went out without another word. Fenya said later that he seemed to be thinking about something with great intensity.

A quarter of an hour later he walked into the rooms of a young official, Pyotr Ilyich Perkhotin, to whom he had pawned his pistols that morning for ten roubles. Perkhotin was startled. Dmitri's hands and face were smeared with blood, and in his right hand he held a thick wad of hundred-rouble notes, which he did not even seem to notice.
“Karamazov! What's happened to you? You're covered in blood! Have you fallen? Look at yourself!”
“Blood? Oh, yes. I was... I was in a fight. I hurt a man, an old man. It's nothing.” He laughed. “I've come to take back my pistols. Here's the money.” He threw the notes on the table.
“But where did you get all that money? This morning you didn't have ten roubles!”
“Never mind where I got it. I have it now. I must go to Mokroye at once. Help me, Pyotr Ilyich. I need champagne, lots of it, and food, and a carriage with three horses.”

Perkhotin made him wash his hands and face. The water in the basin turned red. He noticed that the cuff of Dmitri's right sleeve was soaked with blood too. Dmitri laughed and talked feverishly as he washed, and his mood changed from one second to the next.

They went together to the big shop of Plotnikov, where Dmitri was well known, and he ordered everything: three dozen bottles of champagne, sausages, sweets, cheese, chocolates, pears, sardines, all to be sent after him to Mokroye. He paid with a careless hand from the bundle of notes. Perkhotin, watching him, grew more and more uneasy.
“Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovich, what's going on? Tell me the truth. You're going somewhere to shoot yourself, aren't you? Why do you need the pistols?”

Dmitri laughed. He wrote a few words on a scrap of paper, folded it, and put it in his waistcoat pocket. “I'm going to see the dawn, Pyotr Ilyich, the golden-haired Phoebus. Let me get out of the way. I love life. I've loved life too much, so much that it's disgusting. Enough! Let's drink to life, my friend. And here's to the queen of my soul!”
“Who did you hurt?” asked Perkhotin. “Tell me at least that.”
“An old man. But don't worry about him, I'll pay for it. Goodbye, Pyotr Ilyich. Don't remember evil of me.”
The carriage with three horses arrived at the door, with the driver Andrey. Dmitri jumped in. The bells jingled, and he was off into the night, down the long road to Mokroye.

Perkhotin stood alone outside the shop. “It's none of my business,” he told himself. But he could not forget the blood on Dmitri's hands. He walked home slowly, thinking hard. Then, instead of going to bed, he turned back and went to Grushenka's house to ask a few questions.

chapters.title: The Road to Mokroye
paragraphs: The horses flew down the dark road. Above them the stars shone in the cold, clear sky. Dmitri sat in the cart, silent, and the driver, Andrey, glanced at him from time to time.

It was more than twenty miles to Mokroye, and Dmitri had promised Andrey an extra fifty roubles if he got there in an hour. The road ran through dark fields and little sleeping villages, and the cold wind blew in his face. He thought of nothing and of everything at once. He was aware, all the time, of the folded note in his pocket and of the pistols lying beside him on the seat.

He was going to see her for the last time. He had decided everything. He would not stand in the way of her happiness. Her first lover, the officer, had come back for her, and she had flown to him. Who was he, Dmitri, to stand in their way? He would see her, give them a feast, look at her one last time, and at dawn, when the sun rose, he would go out and shoot himself. The note in his pocket said: I punish myself for my whole life, my whole life I punish.
“Andrey, simple soul,” he suddenly said to the driver, “tell me, will Dmitri Fyodorovich Karamazov go to hell or not?”

“I don't know, sir. It depends on you,” said Andrey. Then he told him a little story he had heard. When Christ came down from the cross, he went straight to hell and set free all the sinners who were suffering there. And hell groaned, because it thought that no one would ever come to it again. And Christ said: Don't groan, hell, for all sorts of important people, governors, judges and rich men, will come to you, and you will be full again, as you have been for all time, until I come again. “That's what they say, sir. But you, sir, are like a little child. The Lord will forgive you for your simplicity.”

“Lord, take me with all my lawlessness,” prayed Dmitri, “but do not judge me. Let me pass without judgement. Do not judge me, for I have judged myself. I love Thee, O Lord. I am a wretch, but I love Thee. Let me love to the end.”

At last they reached Mokroye. The big inn stood at the end of the village, and the windows on the side of the courtyard were lit. The innkeeper, Trifon Borisych, a fat, sly peasant who had made a great deal of money from Dmitri's last visit, came out to meet him and bowed low.
“Is she here, Trifon? Agrafena Alexandrovna?”
“Here, sir. She's here. With some Polish gentlemen. And Mr Kalganov, a young gentleman, and a little old landowner, Maximov. They're playing cards.”

Dmitri crept up to the door of the blue room, where they were all sitting, and looked in through the curtain. Grushenka sat in an armchair by the table. Next to her, on the sofa, sat young Kalganov, a pleasant, handsome boy of twenty. At the table sat two Poles. One, short and stout, with a small moustache and a pipe, was her former lover. The other, very tall, was his friend. Old Maximov, a talkative, pathetic little man, was laughing at something.
Grushenka saw him first. She screamed, and then she laughed. Dmitri came forward, white and trembling, and spoke very fast.

“Gentlemen, I... it's nothing. Don't be afraid. I've come... I want to spend the last night with you here, in this very room. Gentlemen, I'm a traveller, I'm passing through. I only want to drink to your health and leave. I'll go at dawn. Panie, will you allow me?” He turned to the short Pole. “Agrafena Alexandrovna, will you allow me?”

Grushenka was looking at him intently. “Sit down, Mitya. Sit down with us. I'm glad you came,” she said, and her voice was strangely firm. “Do you hear, I'm glad. I want him to stay,” she said to the Pole. “If he goes, I'll go too.”
The Pole bowed stiffly. “If the lady wishes it, then of course.”

chapters.title: The Polish Gentleman
paragraphs: At first everything went badly. Dmitri was nervous, talked too much, laughed too loudly and kept ordering more champagne. The short Pole, Pan Mussyalovich, sat with his pipe and spoke in a pompous mixture of Russian and Polish, correcting everyone and taking offence at everything. The tall Pole, Pan Vrublevsky, said little. Grushenka watched it all with a kind of feverish attention.

“Let's play cards,” said Dmitri at last, to break the silence. The Poles agreed at once. They sent for a new pack, but the tall Pole insisted on taking his own, and soon Dmitri was losing heavily. Kalganov, watching the game, suddenly cried out, “Stop! Don't play any more. They're cheating.”
Dmitri now had another idea. He asked the short Pole to step into the next room for a few words. There, behind closed doors, he made his offer.

“Panie, here's three hundred roubles now. Take them and go away. Leave her. And I'll give you two thousand seven hundred more tomorrow, in town. Three thousand in all. Do you understand? Take it and go.”
The Pole looked at the money with interest. “Three thousand? Give me the three thousand now.”
“I haven't got it all now. But tomorrow...”
The Pole drew himself up with great dignity. “Pan Karamazov, you insult me. Get away!” And he marched back into the blue room.
“Pani Agrippina!” he declared loudly. “This gentleman offered me money to leave you. I am a Polish gentleman. I spit on his money!”

Grushenka turned to him, and there was a terrible look on her face. “And you'd have taken it, if he'd had it all on him,” she said slowly. “Wouldn't you? You'd have taken three thousand, and left me. You came here because you heard I had money. I know it. You came for my money!”
At that moment Trifon Borisych came in and, at Dmitri's request, examined the cards. He found another pack hidden in the tall Pole's pocket, and the cards had been marked. Everyone saw it.
“Cheats!” cried Kalganov.

The Poles shouted in fury. Dmitri, now laughing, simply picked up the tall Pole in his arms, carried him into the next room, put him down and locked the door. The short Pole followed him in a rage, still protesting about his honour.
Grushenka sat very still. Then she covered her face with her hands and began to sob.

“Fool that I was! Five years I tormented myself, and for what? He's not the same man at all. He was like a falcon then, and now he's a drake. His wig, his moustache, his pompous speeches! He's not the one I loved. He's a mean little man. And he came to me to borrow money. I've been crying for five years over nothing, over a dream!”

She raised her head and looked straight at Dmitri. “Mitya, come here. Why did you give me up so easily? Why did you let me go? Did you really mean to give me to him?” Then she cried out, “Bring wine! Bring champagne! Call the girls, call the singers! I want to dance! I want to be drunk!”

chapters.title: A Night of Joy
paragraphs: Within an hour the whole inn was full. The village girls came in their bright dresses, the musicians played their fiddles and balalaikas, the peasants drank vodka at the doors, and the champagne flowed. Old Maximov danced a comic dance. Grushenka drank glass after glass, laughed, sang and clapped her hands. Dmitri moved through it all as if in a dream. Everything seemed to be happening far away.
At last Grushenka took him by the hand and led him behind the curtain into a little room where there was a bed. She sat down and drew him to her.

“Mitya, my falcon, I love you. Do you hear? I love only you. It's you I've loved all along, though I didn't know it. An hour ago I knew. I said to myself: there's my falcon, and here's my drake. Forgive me for tormenting you, my darling. I'm wicked. But I'll love you all my life now. I'll be your slave. We'll go away somewhere, we'll work the land together, far away from everyone.”
“Grusha! My queen! Is it true?” He fell on his knees before her and pressed his face to her lap. “I'll be faithful to you. I'll give my life for you.”

Then, in the middle of his happiness, a sudden shadow fell on his heart. He remembered old Grigory lying by the fence, bleeding. He remembered the money, the three thousand that was not his. He did not know whether the old servant was alive or dead. Joy and horror mixed together in him.
“Grusha, listen, I must tell you... there's something. I'm a thief, and maybe something worse. But I'll make up for it. I'll work for it. Tomorrow I'll tell you everything.”
“Don't tell me anything now,” she whispered. “Tomorrow. Tomorrow we'll begin a new life. Let's be honest, Mitya, honest and good. Let's be good, not beasts. Kiss me.”

Outside, the music went on. Through the window they could see that it was nearly dawn. A cold grey light was beginning to touch the sky. Dmitri sat beside her on the bed, holding her hand, and for one moment he believed that everything could still be saved, that life was beginning, that he would live.

He did not hear the carriages that had stopped quietly in the yard. He did not hear the heavy steps in the passage, or the low voices of men giving orders to Trifon Borisych. Grushenka had fallen asleep, her head on the pillow, with a smile on her lips. Dmitri was sitting by her, half dozing, when suddenly she opened her eyes.
“Mitya, I had a dream. I dreamt we were driving over the snow, and I was so happy... What's that noise? Who's there?”
The curtain was pulled aside.

chapters.title: What Happened in Town
paragraphs: While Dmitri was racing towards Mokroye, Pyotr Ilyich Perkhotin had been asking questions. At Grushenka's house he found Fenya still trembling in the kitchen. She told him everything: how Dmitri had come in like a madman, how he had seized the brass pestle from the table and run off, and how he had come back half an hour later with blood on his hands and asked where Grushenka was.
“The pestle?” said Perkhotin. “And when he came back, did he have it?”
“No, sir. He came back without it. I looked, sir, I looked at once. He didn't have it.”
Perkhotin grew cold. He remembered the wad of notes in Dmitri's bloody hand. “The man was penniless this morning,” he thought. “Now he has thousands. And he talked about an old man he had hurt.”

He did not dare go straight to the police. What if it was all nonsense? He would look like a fool. So he went first to Madame Khokhlakova, to ask whether she had given Dmitri any money, as he had said she had. It was nearly midnight, and the lady was already in bed, but at last she agreed to see him.

“Three thousand roubles? I gave him nothing! Nothing at all! I advised him to go to the gold mines. I gave him a little icon. And he ran out shouting. Oh, Pyotr Ilyich, he's killed someone! I knew it! I felt it! Go to the police at once. He'll kill us all!”

She wrote him a note, declaring that she had never given Dmitri Karamazov any money, and Perkhotin, now really alarmed, went to the house of the police captain, Mikhail Makarovich. To his surprise he found the whole household awake and in a state of great agitation. The police captain, the prosecutor Ippolit Kirillovich, the young examining magistrate Nikolai Parfenovich and the district doctor were all there, getting ready to leave.
Terrible news had arrived only a little earlier from Fyodor Pavlovich's house.

Marfa Ignatievna, Grigory's wife, had woken up in the night to the sound of a dreadful cry from the next room, where Smerdyakov lay ill. It was the scream he always gave at the start of a fit. Then she noticed that her husband was not in his bed. She went out into the dark garden calling him, and she heard a groan from near the fence. She found him lying there, with his head covered in blood, barely alive.

Grigory managed to whisper a few words before he lost consciousness again. “He's killed him... his father... killed... call the master... Parricide!” Marfa ran screaming to the house. She saw that the window of the master's bedroom was wide open and the light was burning. She looked in, and what she saw made her run, shrieking, to the neighbours.

Fyodor Pavlovich lay on his back on the floor of his bedroom, in his silk dressing gown and clean white shirt, with his head smashed in. There was blood everywhere. The weapon was not in the room, but later, in the garden, near the place where Grigory had fallen, they found a brass pestle in the grass.

On the floor of the bedroom, beside the body, lay a large, thick envelope of good paper, torn open and empty. On it was written, in Fyodor Pavlovich's own hand: A gift of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she will come. And below, in smaller writing: and to my little chicken. Near it lay a thin pink ribbon.

Smerdyakov was found in his bed, twisting in the most terrible fit, and the doctor said he would probably not survive the night. Grigory said, when he came round, that he had seen the garden door of the house standing wide open before he saw a figure running away in the dark. He was sure the figure was Dmitri Fyodorovich.

No one in the town had any doubt about who had done it. Everyone had heard Dmitri threaten his father. Everyone knew about his hatred, his jealousy, his need for money. Now Perkhotin came in with his story of the blood, the wad of notes and the pestle taken from Grushenka's kitchen, and of Dmitri's mad drive to Mokroye with his pistols.
“To Mokroye, then,” said the prosecutor. “At once. He may shoot himself before we get there.”

Before dawn, two carriages left the town at full speed, carrying the police captain, the prosecutor, the examining magistrate, a secretary and several constables. They reached the inn while the music was still playing. They stopped in the yard and spoke quietly to Trifon Borisych, and they placed men at every door.

chapters.title: The Arrest
paragraphs: The curtain was pulled aside, and Dmitri saw a tall, heavy man in an overcoat and a cap with a badge. Behind him stood several other figures. For a moment Dmitri did not understand. Then he recognised the police captain, Mikhail Makarovich, and beside him the prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovich, a thin, sickly man with a pale face, and the young examining magistrate, Nikolai Parfenovich, with his rings on his fingers and his gold spectacles. In the doorway were a peasant constable and Trifon Borisych, looking frightened.
Dmitri stood up slowly. “What is it? What do you want, gentlemen?”

“Retired Lieutenant Karamazov,” said the police captain loudly, in a voice that shook a little, “I must inform you that you are accused of the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov, committed this night.”
Dmitri looked from one to another. His mind was a blank. “The murder of my father? The old man... his blood?”
“Yes, sir. Your father was found dead in his bedroom tonight. And his servant Grigory was found in the garden with his head broken.”
Dmitri gazed at them wildly. Then, suddenly, an extraordinary expression came over his face, an expression almost of joy, though no one in the room understood it.

“The old man's blood! I understand, I understand! But gentlemen... I'm not guilty of it! I'm not guilty of my father's blood. I wanted to kill him, but I'm not guilty. Not I! Grigory, though... I hit Grigory. Is he alive?”
Grushenka had jumped up from the bed. She threw herself between Dmitri and the officials, and then she fell on her knees before them, stretching out her arms.

“It's my fault! I'm the one who's guilty!” she cried. “I tormented him and drove him to it. I tormented that poor old man too, out of spite, and brought him to this. It's my fault, mine first, mine most of all!”
“Yes, you're guilty! You're the chief criminal! You fury, you harlot! You're the most guilty of all!” shouted the police captain, shaking his fist at her. But the others quickly made him be quiet.
“Gentlemen, she's not guilty! She knows nothing!” cried Dmitri. “Don't touch her, don't insult her! I'll answer for everything myself. I'll tell you everything. Only leave her alone.”

They led Grushenka out of the room, gently but firmly. As she went, she turned and looked at Dmitri with eyes full of tears. “Mitya, my darling, whatever happens, I'm with you. Don't believe that I'll leave you. I'll follow you to the end of the world, even if they condemn you!”

The constables took up their positions. Trifon Borisych closed the doors, and the music in the hall stopped. The village girls were sent home. In the grey light of dawn, the guests stood about in silence, Kalganov pale and upset, old Maximov in tears. The Polish gentlemen had locked themselves in their room.

Dmitri sat down heavily at the table where, a few hours earlier, the champagne had been flowing. He looked at the empty glasses and the scattered cards. He looked at the faces of the men around him, cold, official, curious. In the corner, the secretary was spreading out his papers and dipping his pen in the ink.

“Gentlemen,” said Dmitri, with a sudden shaky laugh, “I've been a fool. I came here to shoot myself at dawn, and the dawn has come, and instead... Well. Ask your questions. I'm ready. I'll show you that I'm innocent. It'll all be over in five minutes, you'll see. We'll laugh about it afterwards.”
The prosecutor exchanged a glance with the magistrate. Nikolai Parfenovich smiled politely and took off his spectacles to polish them.
“We shall be very glad to hear everything you have to say, Dmitri Fyodorovich,” he said. “Let us begin.”

Outside, the sun was rising over Mokroye, red and cold, the same sun that Dmitri had meant to greet with a bullet. Instead, a long and terrible ordeal was beginning, and no one in that room, least of all Dmitri himself, could yet imagine where it would end.
